subject: nonlinear association between covariates and dependent variable (outcome)

messages.author: 3fa01d1518fb40c4
messages.subject: nonlinear association between covariates and dependent variable (outcome)
parts:
Hello everyone,

 

I’m a student from China, I have a question now. I am now doing a spatio-temporal model, and I want to put some climate covariates in the model, just as follows:

 

formula <- y ~ 1+ x1+ x2+ x3 + f(ID.area,model="bym",graph=Georgia.adj) +f(ID.year,model="rw2")


result <- inla(formula, family='poisson', … …)


x1,x2,x3 are the climate covariates I want to put in.

But the association between climate variables and dependent variable y is nonlinear.

So the formula y ~ 1+ x1+ x2+ x3 +… … is not suitable.

Should I use spline function or GAMs in x1,x2,x3? And how to set these functions in code in the R-INLA package?

Or other suggestions?


Sincerely thanks for your help.

 

Yours,

Yijing

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] nonlinear association between covariates and dependent variable (outcome)
parts:
Hi,
One common way to model nonlinear covariate effects is the one you already use for time; rw2 (which is essentially a spline model).

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] nonlinear association between covariates and dependent variable (outcome)
parts:
Yes, the rw2 model is defined so that it behaves like a continuous model. (The documentation I think refers to “irregular spacing” which is precisely used for this. There’s a Lindgren&Rue paper in the Scandinavian Journal of Statistics from 2008 that explains it:
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9469.2008.00610.x/abstract

Finn

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] nonlinear association between covariates and dependent variable (outcome)
parts:
Yes, it would give a piecewise constant model. It would make the continuous variable discrete. If you have "enough" bins, however, discrete and continuous is numerically the same.

I think the usual approach with RW2 is
1. 20 bins is an ok first try
2. Use more bins if it looks like you need it (by looking at the posterior)
3. Check sensitivity with respect to number of bins chosen (when you report the results)

If I were to recommend an approach with "good properties"
- Use the 1-dimensional mesh as Finn suggests. 
- I would also use Matern instead of RW2, since this model is proper.

Kind regards,
Haakon
